wasm-html-to-image/markdown converts GitHub-flavoured Markdown (GFM) into beautifully styled HTML pages and multi-page PDF documents. It is implemented in pure JavaScript with no Node.js platform dependencies, running seamlessly across Node.js, modern browsers, and edge runtimes like Cloudflare Workers.

markdownToDocument() & markdownToHtml(): Produce HTML and complete PDF render options (headers, footers, metadata). Template System: 11 built-in templates (default, report, proposal, book, paper, compact, manual, minutes, letter, slides, invoice) for ready-to-use professional styling without writing CSS. Automatic Table of Contents (TOC): Generates a table of contents with exact destination page numbers filled in during PDF pagination. Automatic PDF Bookmarks (Outline): Creates nested PDF document outlines from h1–h6 headings. Smart Page Break Handling: Avoids orphan headings (break-after: avoid) and prevents breaking code blocks and tables across page boundaries. YAML Front Matter: Parses document metadata (title, subtitle, author, date, template, stamp, cover, accent, etc.). Syntax Highlighting: Built-in highlight.js covering 20+ programming languages. Mermaid diagrams: ```mermaid blocks are drawn inside the engine (flowchart, sequence, state, class, ER, Gantt, pie and more: over 30 kinds; see the list). KaTeX Mathematical Typesetting (/markdown-math): High-accuracy rendering for inline $…$ and display $$…$$ equations.

Use markdownToDocument() to retrieve both the document HTML and the required PDF options (such as running headers and footers), then pass them to render(): import fs from "node:fs/promises"; import { render } from "wasm-html-to-image"; import { markdownToDocument } from "wasm-html-to-image/markdown"; const md = `--- title: Quarterly Performance Report subtitle: Q3 2026 author: Taro Yamada date: 2026-10-29 template: report accent: "#2563eb" stamp: CONFIDENTIAL --- # Executive Summary Revenue increased by **+15.2%** year-over-year. # Key Performance Indicators | KPI | Target | Actual | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Gross Margin | $5.0M | $5.4M | | New Customers | 120 | 135 | `; // Retrieve HTML and PDF layout options const { html, renderOptions } = markdownToDocument(md, { paged: true, // Enable page margins and pagination optimization }); const { data } = await render({ value: html, format: "pdf", ...renderOptions, }); await fs.writeFile("report.pdf", Buffer.from(data));

Use markdownToHtml() when rendering standalone images: import { render } from "wasm-html-to-image"; import { markdownToHtml } from "wasm-html-to-image/markdown"; const html = markdownToHtml("# Document Title\n\nContent...", { theme: "dark", maxWidth: 800, }); const { data } = await render({ value: html, width: 900, format: "png", });

Option Type Default Description template string | MarkdownTemplate none A bundled template by name, or your own (see Custom Templates). Wins over the front matter's template: settings DocumentSettings none Document settings that override the front matter (title, author, accent, font, page_size, cover, stamp, ...) theme "light" | "dark" "light" Colour scheme of the built-in stylesheet css string none Extra CSS appended after the built-in stylesheet stylesheet string none Replace the built-in stylesheet entirely (theme is then ignored) paged boolean false For PDF: padding becomes the @page margin on every page, so pages after the first keep their top and bottom margins padding number 32 Space around the article, px maxWidth number none Maximum width of the article, px; omitted means the full viewport width title string front matter title <title> of the document toc boolean | { depth?: number, title?: string } on for PDF (paged) Table of contents. depth 1–6 (default 3); title is the heading above it (default Contents, empty leaves it out) highlight boolean true Syntax-highlight code blocks that name a language mermaid boolean true Draw ```mermaid as diagrams; false leaves them as code blocks frontMatter boolean true Strip a leading YAML front matter block and read its title math MathRenderer none Typeset $…$ / $$…$$: pass katexMath() from wasm-html-to-image/markdown-math. Without it a dollar sign is just text markdownToDocument() returns { html, settings, renderOptions }. settings is what applied (template defaults < front matter < options); renderOptions are the PDF options to spread into render() (header, footer, pdfTitle, pdfAuthor, pdfBackground, pdfSkipRunning). markdownStylesheet() returns just the CSS of the built-in stylesheet.

Templates configure the document's typography, page size, margins, running headers/footers, and cover/contents pages. All templates support both light and dark themes. Place front matter at the top of the file enclosed by ---: --- title: System Architecture Spec
v2.0 subtitle: Next-generation Graphics Pipeline author: Core Engineering Team date: 2026-10-29 template: report accent: "#059669" font: sans-serif page_size: A4 stamp: DRAFT cover: true toc: true logo: https://example.com/logo.png lang: en ---
Settings are resolved in the following order: Template defaults (template.defaults) Front matter attributes API options (options.settings, options.title, etc.)

These front matter keys also change the page: Key Value Effect header / footer HTML Running header and footer (replacing the template's). {{title}}, {{author}}, {{date}}, {{stamp}}, {{pageNumber}}, {{totalPages}} and {{chapter}} (the h1 the page shows first, else the chapter before it) work. The book header shows the chapter margin 20mm 18mm Page margin (a CSS margin value) orientation landscape Turn the paper sideways toc_depth 1 to 6 Deepest heading level in the contents toc_title text Heading of the contents page (Contents) cover_style band / plain / center Look of the cover numbering true Number the headings 1, 1.1, 1.1.1 footnotes end Where footnotes go: end lists them after the text, page sets each at the foot of the page that refers to it (PDF; if one note is taller than a third of a page, the list stays at the end) mermaid_theme a name (nord, ...) Draw the diagrams with a named theme instead of the document's light / dark colours (pick one that suits the page: dracula, nord or dark on a dark document) mermaid_mode compat / recover How much a broken diagram is forgiven mermaid_directives true Honour %%{init}%% and frontmatter inside the diagrams With a template that has a cover, the cover carries no header or footer (page numbers still count it as page 1).

Call-outs: a block quote that starts with [!NOTE], [!TIP], [!IMPORTANT], [!WARNING] or [!CAUTION] becomes a coloured box (the title is Japanese with lang: ja). Numbered figures: an image with a title, ![alt](src "Title"), becomes a figure captioned Figure 1 Title. Page break: <!-- pagebreak --> forces a new page. Footnotes: [^name] in the text and [^name]: the note anywhere put a list of notes at the end, numbered by first use. Tables span the text width in report, proposal, book and paper. Long code lines wrap at the right edge instead of being cut.

When paged: true (or CLI PDF output) is specified: Contents Page: Headings down to level 3 (by default) are indexed. Page numbers are dynamically linked to the layout output. Bookmarks (Outline): Headings h1–h6 automatically form the PDF reader outline tree. In-page Links: Links such as [details](#setup) work seamlessly inside the PDF. // Customise depth and heading const { html, renderOptions } = markdownToDocument(md, { paged: true, toc: { depth: 2, title: "Contents" }, }); // Disable TOC page const { html, renderOptions } = markdownToDocument(md, { paged: true, toc: false, }); // Disable PDF bookmarks await render({ value: html, format: "pdf", pdfOutline: false, ...renderOptions, });

Put the name of a bundled template in extends and override its type, page and defaults field by field; your css is appended after the base's. defineTemplate() only type-checks and returns the value unchanged. import { defineTemplate, markdownToDocument } from "wasm-html-to-image/markdown"; const mine = defineTemplate({ extends: "report", type: { size: 13 }, defaults: { accent: "#0f766e" }, css: ".markdown-body h2 { border-bottom-style: dashed; }", }); const doc = markdownToDocument(md, { template: mine, paged: true }); From the CLI, a JSON file such as { "extends": "report", "defaults": { "accent": "#0f766e" } } works with --template mine.json.
In a template's css, use var(--surface), var(--border), var(--muted), var(--text) and var(--accent) instead of fixed colours, so the template follows both the light and the dark theme.

The engine draws Mermaid diagrams itself, as vectors. No browser, Puppeteer or Mermaid JavaScript is needed. There are three ways to use it. Way Entry Good for A ```mermaid fence in Markdown wasm-html-to-image/markdown Diagrams inside a document; they go into the PDF as they are <pre class="mermaid"> / <div class="mermaid"> in HTML render() A diagram inside an HTML page The diagram alone renderMermaid() An SVG string or a PNG (or other image) of one diagram All three use the same engine and the same diagram types. Text is measured with the real fonts, so Japanese labels fit exactly.

```mermaid graph LR A[Order] --> B{In stock?} B -->|yes| C[Ship] B -->|no| D[Reorder] ``` In a PDF a diagram is never split across pages, and its text stays selectable vector text. Pass mermaid: false to show it as an ordinary code block. See Markdown Conversion for more.

sequenceDiagram A->>B: Hello 
 works the same. The element's text is the diagram source. Colours and behaviour come from the page's CSS (CSS control). Write the source as text: escape < and & (A --> B). With no theme and no --mermaid-bg / --mermaid-surface / --mermaid-fg, a diagram on a dark page (the nearest opaque background is dark; with none, the text colour is light) takes the dark theme automatically, keeping the page's color for text. On a light page the colours come from the element's color. For another look set --mermaid-theme: nord; (or another theme). The diagram sits among the other elements as a block.

Give a .mmd / .mermaid file and the output is an image (or SVG, or PDF) sized to the diagram; the extension of -o picks the format. npx wasm-html-to-image flow.mmd -o flow.svg npx wasm-html-to-image flow.mmd -o flow.png --mermaid-theme nord npx wasm-html-to-image "graph LR; A-->B" --mermaid -o ab.png # inline text cat flow.mmd | npx wasm-html-to-image - --mermaid -o flow.webp --mermaid-mode recover The image width is fixed only when you pass -w. --accent sets the arrow colour and --mermaid-directives honours %%{init}%% in the source.

Entry renderMermaid wasm-html-to-image/single (and wasm-html-to-image on Node.js and similar) Yes wasm-html-to-image/workers Yes (drawn on the worker pool) /workerd (on Cloudflare Workers wasm-html-to-image resolves here too) Yes, bound to the bundled WASM /edge-light No renderMermaid; draw with render({ mermaid: { source, ... }, format }, wasm) renderMermaid(source, options) is shorthand for render({ mermaid: { source, ...options }, format, width }). The render of every entry takes mermaid: { source, theme, padding, mode, directives, accent, background, onWarning, ... }. width and format are render options, and the other options (fontMap, limits, onLog, ...) reach the drawing as they are. import { render } from "wasm-html-to-image"; // the theme can be chosen on every call of render const { data } = await render({ mermaid: { source: "graph LR
 A --> B", theme: "nord", accent: "#ff79c6" }, format: "png", }); The theme names are the type MermaidTheme and the list MERMAID_THEMES, both importable from wasm-html-to-image (Themes). An unknown theme name throws an error that lists the names you can use. onWarning is called for render on the worker pool (/workers) too. mermaidToHtml(source, options) returns an HTML string with one diagram, for when you want a page.

The layout of a big graph grows faster than its size (measured: a flowchart takes seconds at 600 nodes and minutes at 1500). So that a server that draws whatever a user sends cannot be stalled by one huge diagram, there are limits on lines (default 2000) and on source size (default 200000 bytes). A syntax error or an unsupported diagram shows as a one-line error box (Mermaid: ...) where the diagram would be; the rest of the document still converts. renderMermaid() returns an SVG of the same box.

Option Type Description javascript boolean | { timeout?: number, settleMs?: number, waitFor?: string, engine?: "quickjs", limits?, skip? } Run the page's <script>s in QuickJS (WebAssembly) on a DOM written in C before rendering (the Node.js single entry and the CLI's --js do it for you; on edge entries, call applyJavaScript() first). true waits 1 s after load. timeout bounds the whole phase (default 10000 ms; 0 / Infinity disables the limit), settleMs is the wait after load (default 1000 ms), waitFor is a CSS selector to wait for (replaces settleMs). engine accepts only "quickjs" (kept for one release; "jsdom" throws at runtime) — there is no other engine. limits / skip bound what the page may fetch. There is no layout and no sandbox: use it with trusted pages only mermaid { source, theme?, padding?, background?, accent?, mode?, directives?, onWarning?, maxLines?, maxSourceBytes? } Draw a Mermaid diagram (instead of value), as an image sized to the diagram. See Mermaid conversion Running scripts on edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers and others)​ The QuickJS (WebAssembly) engine runs on every runtime. Where eval is not allowed, such as Workers, applyJavaScript() from wasm-html-to-image/javascript runs the page's scripts in QuickJS on a DOM written in C. A React / Next.js client has been checked to run through hydration and its useEffects. import { applyJavaScript } from "wasm-html-to-image/javascript"; import { render } from "wasm-html-to-image/workerd"; const options = await applyJavaScript({ url: "https://example.com/", javascript: true, width: 1200, format: "png" }); const { data } = await render(options); The package picks the QuickJS wasm for the runtime (#quickjs-wasm in the imports of package.json): a pre-compiled module on Workers and on Vercel / Next.js Edge, read from disk on Node.js and Bun, fetched on Deno and in browsers. To use a module of your own, pass it as applyJavaScript(options, { quickjsWasm }). The Node.js single entry and the CLI's --js run the same phase for you. The engine itself is the separate package wasm-quickjs-dom (a small DOM implementation that knows nothing about images), installed as a dependency of wasm-html-to-image. createDOM can also be used straight from wasm-quickjs-dom. The Node.js single entry's runPageScripts is now an alias of wasm-quickjs-dom's runPageScriptsQuickJS. Its third argument viewportWidth defaults to undefined (the options' width is used, then 800) instead of 800, so matchMedia can answer differently than before. Limits: no layout of its own (getBoundingClientRect returns 0 until measureLayout() or enableLiveLayout() supplies boxes; see below), no canvas, type="module" scripts run, but only imports with literal specifiers (fetched up front) resolve. The DOM is a small one written in C, and QuickJS is an interpreter, so heavy pages are slower. More limits: attachShadow() works, but serialize() and the rendered HTML leave shadow trees out (a warning is logged when a root is attached). document.fonts is a stub (ready resolves at once, check() is always true, load() resolves to an empty array) and FontFace does not exist. Interaction pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus, :active, :visited, :target, :focus-within, :focus-visible) and pseudo-elements never match, in selectors or in getComputedStyle() (matchMedia("(hover: hover)") still reports true). document.elementFromPoint() returns null and elementsFromPoint() returns []; scroll(), scrollTo(), scrollBy(), and scrollIntoView() do nothing (scrollTop / scrollLeft read 0). An <iframe>'s contentWindow / contentDocument are null, and srcdoc is kept as an attribute only, never loaded. XPath cannot resolve namespace prefixes (namespace-uri() is "", createNSResolver() returns null). crypto.getRandomValues() / crypto.randomUUID() are built on Math.random, so they are not cryptographically secure. Canvas getContext() returns null (and toDataURL() "data:,"), so calling a method on the context throws a TypeError. SVG getBBox() / getTotalLength() / getPointAtLength() are approximate: a path's A command is its chord, transforms are ignored, and <text> is 0 × 0. Use it with trusted pages only (the scripts can fetch). For pages you do not control, always add the fetch limits below, or javascript: { limits, skip }. IntersectionObserver and ResizeObserver report once when you observe() (the page is meant to be seen whole, without scrolling, so everything counts as intersecting and lazy content gets to load). matchMedia answers for the viewport width (min-width / max-width / orientation ..., with a light-mode, no-motion user). getComputedStyle computes the cascade of <style> and the element's own style, inheritance and initial values, but does not lay out: a width / height of auto or % comes back as written (auto, 50%, ...), so take real sizes from the boxes measureLayout() returns. Keeping the DOM open (createDOM)​ Without rendering anything, the page can be kept open and driven, like a browser page. The DOM lives inside QuickJS, so you talk to it through eval() and JSON values rather than a live dom.window. import { createDOM } from "wasm-html-to-image/javascript"; import { render } from "wasm-html-to-image/workerd"; const dom = await createDOM({ url: "https://example.com/" }, { width: 1200 }); try { const title = await dom.eval("document.title"); // the value comes back as JSON; promises are awaited await dom.eval("document.querySelector('h1').textContent = 'Hello'"); const { data } = await render(dom.toOptions({ width: 1200, format: "png" })); // draw the DOM as it is now } finally { dom.close(); // frees QuickJS } eval(fn, ...args) also takes a function and JSON arguments (dom.eval((sel) => document.querySelectorAll(sel).length, "a")). The function travels as source text, so it cannot use variables from its surroundings. click(selector), type(selector, text) (sets value, fires input and change) and waitForSelector(selector) drive the page and wait for it. They return false when nothing matched. expose(name, fn) makes a host function callable from the page as await window[name](...args). Arguments and result travel as JSON; a throw becomes a rejection with the same message. eval(code) runs code in the page's global scope and returns the result as JSON. A promise is awaited, and what the code throws becomes an Error. A DOM node cannot be returned: return what you read from it. Calls run one after another. settle(ms?) lets the page's timers and fetches run. The page's clock runs only during eval() / settle(), not in between. serialize() is the current HTML; toOptions(options) gives render options you can pass to render() as they are. The second argument of createDOM is the javascript option (timeout / settleMs / waitFor) plus width and quickjsWasm. timeout counts per call. bridge() gives the host synchronous access to the page's DOM (each property read, write or method call is one call into QuickJS; the same node is always the same wrapper). Moving from jsdom: the DOM lives inside QuickJS, so there is no window to hand around. Values cross the boundary as JSON, so dom.eval(fn, ...args) returns only what JSON can carry (no DOM nodes), and a function travels as source text, so it cannot close over outer variables. Give the page host functions with dom.expose(name, fn) (await window[name](...args)), and use dom.bridge() when the host wants to touch the DOM itself. There is no beforeParse hook: prepend a <script> to the HTML, or eval() your setup into the page after createDOM() and let settle() carry it into the page's pending work. Command line: npx wasm-quickjs-dom <URL | file | -> prints the HTML after the scripts ran (-e prints a value, --json adds the logs, --wait / --settle / --timeout, and the limits --block-private / --allow-host / --skip ...). --help lists everything. Speed: with the QuickJS engine settleMs is an upper bound. With no timer pending that falls due within it and no request in flight the page can no longer change, so it finishes without using up the time. External <script src>s are requested all at once and only run in document order. skip: (url) => boolean fails the URLs a render does not need (analytics, ads, ...) without going to the network (a <script> gets its error event, a fetch rejects). On real sites these three take most of the time off. Fetch limits (limits): for pages you do not control, restrict where the page's scripts may fetch from. It covers the page's own fetch / XMLHttpRequest, the <script>s and modules it loads, and the page itself given as url. const dom = await createDOM({ url }, { limits: { allowedProtocols: ["https:"], allowedHosts: ["example.com", "cdn.example.com"], // exact match blockPrivateHosts: true, // refuse localhost and private, loopback and link-local addresses maxResourceCount: 50, maxResourceBytes: 5_000_000, maxTotalResourceBytes: 20_000_000, }, }); The names are those of the limits of render(). With applyJavaScript() the limits of the same call are the defaults, and javascript: { limits } overrides them. With host or protocol limits, redirects are not followed automatically: each one is checked before it is followed. A runtime that hides the redirect target (a browser's opaqueredirect) cannot be checked, so the request is refused. blockPrivateHosts looks at hostnames and IP literals only. A hostname that resolves to an internal address through DNS cannot be told apart here: pair it with allowedHosts when the target is not trusted. What happened in the page (logs): dom.logs keeps the console output, script errors, unhandled promise rejections (unhandledrejection) and the page's requests with their status or the reason they failed (the last 1000). The onLog option delivers them as they happen. Use them to find out why a page rendered empty. const dom = await createDOM({ url }, { onLog: (e) => e.type === "error" && console.error(e.source, e.message) }); console.log(dom.logs.filter((e) => e.type === "request" && (e.error || (e.status ?? 0) >= 400))); Giving the page a layout (measureLayout): there is no layout inside QuickJS, so getBoundingClientRect() returns 0. measureLayout() lays the page out with the image engine (nothing is drawn or encoded) and hands the numbers to the page. Afterwards getBoundingClientRect(), getClientRects(), offsetWidth / offsetHeight / offsetLeft / offsetTop, clientWidth / clientHeight and scrollWidth / scrollHeight answer with the measured values. import { createDOM, measureLayout } from "wasm-html-to-image/javascript"; import { render } from "wasm-html-to-image/workerd"; const dom = await createDOM({ url: "https://example.com/" }, { width: 1200 }); await measureLayout(dom, render, { width: 1200 }); // the render of the entry you use const h = await dom.eval("document.querySelector('main').getBoundingClientRect().height"); The values are a snapshot: call measureLayout() again after the page changed. An inline element in a line of text (<span>, <a>, ...) gets the one box that encloses all the line fragments it is broken into. The offsets are measured from the top left of the page, not from an offsetParent. The page itself is not touched: the marks for the layout are only on a copy. Following the page's changes (enableLiveLayout): when the page's scripts change the DOM and read getBoundingClientRect() or getComputedStyle() as they go, use enableLiveLayout() instead of the measureLayout() snapshot: every read is answered from the image engine's layout of the page as it is at that moment. The engine keeps the laid-out document and applies only what the page changed (attributes, style, text, inserted / removed / moved nodes). import { createDOM, enableLiveLayout } from "wasm-html-to-image/javascript"; import { getDefaultModule } from "wasm-html-to-image/workerd"; // Node.js: loadHtmlToImageModule() const dom = await createDOM({ url: "https://example.com/" }, { width: 1200 }); const layout = await enableLiveLayout(dom, await getDefaultModule(), { width: 1200, maxElements: 10000 }); await dom.eval("document.querySelector('main').style.height = '400px'"); await dom.eval("document.querySelector('footer').getBoundingClientRect().y"); // already moved await layout.refreshResources(); // fetch the images, style sheets and fonts a script added layout.dispose(); dom.close(); Reads are synchronous and cannot fetch. Style sheets, fonts and images are fetched once, from the page as it is when you call enableLiveLayout(); what a script adds later is fetched by await layout.refreshResources() (until then an added image lays out as empty). Cost of one change plus one read (Node.js, 6,000 elements): a paint-only change (color, ...) about 13 ms, append about 90 ms, a change that moves boxes (height) about 170 ms; it grows with the number of elements. Tables are slower: about 0.6 s per change at 1,500 rows. On Cloudflare Workers (128 MB for both wasm modules) about 13,000 elements fit; keep maxElements at 10,000 or less. A page over it, or an engine failure, leaves the boxes at 0 with one warning and the page keeps running. It needs the compatibility flag enable_weak_ref, and the gzipped upload (about 5.5 MB) needs a paid plan. Design and measurements: doc/design/live-layout-incremental.md; benchmark: packages/html-to-image/scripts/bench-live-layout.mjs.

wasm-html-to-image merges an HTML layout/rendering pipeline and an image optimization/encoding pipeline into a single native WebAssembly binary. Traditional setups require two separate libraries: one rendering HTML to PNG, and another re-encoding PNG to WebP or AVIF. This causes substantial memory allocations and data copying across JavaScript boundaries. wasm-html-to-image eliminates this overhead by piping the rendered Bitmap directly to the encoder within the single Skia-WASM module.

Resource Discovery (satoru_collect_resources): Parses image URLs, @font-face rules, and CSS backgrounds from HTML/CSS. Resource Injection (satoru_add_resource): TypeScript fetches needed resources concurrently using in-memory process caches. Layout & Painting: litehtml computes the box layout, HarfBuzz/SkUnicode shapes text, and Skia renders to an off-screen surface. Output Generation: svg / pdf: Skia streams vector commands directly. Raster formats: Rendered Bitmap is piped straight to native encoders without leaving WASM linear memory.

When given image buffers or data URLs: Direct Decoding: Bypasses the HTML layout engine completely. Transformations: Applies width, height, fit, and crop directly in the image pipeline. Encoding: Compresses to WebP, AVIF, JXL, JPEG, RAW pixels, or ThumbHash.

wasm-html-to-image is a lightweight static renderer based on litehtml and Skia, not a headless browser. Keep the following constraints in mind when writing templates: No JavaScript by default: <script> tags, DOM event listeners, and DOM APIs do not run. The javascript option (CLI: --js) runs the page's scripts in QuickJS (WebAssembly) on a DOM written in C and renders the resulting DOM (the Node.js single entry and the CLI do it for you; on edge entries, use applyJavaScript() from wasm-html-to-image/javascript). The same engine works where eval is not allowed, such as Cloudflare Workers (trusted pages only; see render() options). Scripts that depend on browser-only APIs or layout measurements will not behave as in a browser. Partial CSS Animation Support: transition is not evaluated. @keyframes are ignored by default (only static styles paint), but passing animation: { duration, fps, loop } (CLI: --animation) samples opacity, transform and color / background-color @keyframes into an animated WebP / APNG / GIF. The repeat count is set with loop (CLI: --animation-loop, default 0 = infinite). Defaults are 15 fps with caps of 5 s (duration is clamped to 5000 ms) / ~75 frames. The CSS animation-duration (including the animation shorthand, var() supported) is the length of one iteration; together with animation-delay and animation-iteration-count (a number or infinite) it defines the sampled timeline (infinite samples one iteration, alternate / alternate-reverse two). The API duration is an upper bound on the whole timeline and the API fps caps the frame rate. transform supports translate / rotate / scale only; when the function list differs between the keyframes the element keeps its static transform. An animation-timing-function inside a keyframe block applies to the interval that starts at that stop, and the element-level one (<style> or inline) is the default (linear / ease / ease-in / ease-out / ease-in-out / cubic-bezier() / steps() / step-start / step-end; applied to opacity, color and transform interpolation). animation-direction (normal / reverse / alternate / alternate-reverse) and animation-fill-mode (none / forwards / backwards / both) are honoured, so the value during animation-delay (backwards) and after the animation (forwards) is resolved; a negative animation-delay starts inside the first iteration. Every @keyframes block of the document animates all the elements its rule selects (several allowed); several animations on one element (animation: a 2s, b 3s or animation-name: a, b) are layered, the later one winning on shared properties; translateX / translateY are supported too. NO Canvas Scripting: <canvas> element 2D/WebGL contexts do not execute. Use inline <svg> or CSS shapes instead. NO Interactive States: :hover, :active, and :focus states do not trigger. NO Browser Web Storage: window, document, localStorage, and IndexedDB are unavailable.

wasm-html-to-image is an ultra-fast, self-contained HTML-to-image and image conversion engine that consolidates an HTML rendering engine (Satoru) and an image optimization engine (wasm-image-optimization) into a single WebAssembly (Emscripten) module. It requires no heavy headless browsers like Chromium, Puppeteer, or Playwright, and runs portably across server-side runtimes, edge environments such as Cloudflare Workers, browsers, and the CLI.

Single Unified WASM Module: Parses HTML, calculates CSS layout, renders with Skia, and encodes images (WebP/AVIF/JPEG, etc.) inside one binary without passing intermediate frame buffers across JS boundaries. Versatile Inputs: Supports HTML strings, HTML string arrays (for multi-page PDF), Markdown, URLs, and raw image buffers (PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, AVIF, BMP, Data URLs). Multiple Output Formats: Direct SVG vector output, high-quality PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, raw pixels, ThumbHash, and multi-page PDF generation. Zero-Config render(): Import directly from wasm-html-to-image and render immediately without manual WASM loading or setup (automatically resolves workerd in Cloudflare Workers). Edge & Cloudflare Workers Ready: Along with auto-detection, dedicated wasm-html-to-image/workerd and edge-light subpaths fit constrained serverless edge environments. Parallel Worker Pool: Built-in multi-threaded pool in wasm-html-to-image/workers allows batch generation without stalling the main event loop. Rich Ecosystem Integration: Seamless JSX rendering for React and Preact, UnoCSS-based Tailwind CSS utility classes, and Markdown to image / beautiful PDF documents (templates, automatic TOC, bookmarks, and KaTeX math).

Requires CMake and Emscripten SDK: cmake -B build -S . -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=$EMSDK/upstream/emscripten/cmake/Modules/Platform/Emscripten.cmake cmake --build build --target html-to-image Building with the pnpm scripts​ Usually you use these scripts. The output is packages/html-to-image/dist/html-to-image.wasm. pnpm wasm:build # release build (with ThinLTO; this is what you ship) pnpm wasm:build:dev # development build (no ThinLTO) The development build leaves out only link-time optimisation (ThinLTO), so relinking after a one-line C++ change takes seconds instead of minutes. The optimisation level stays at -O3 (lowering it, for example to -O1, breaks the embind glue). The binary is larger and a little slower. Both builds write to the same place, so always rebuild with pnpm wasm:build before you publish. The flags are set again on every run, so switching between the two does not rebuild more than it has to. After rebuilding the WASM, rebuild the package that embeds it. If you do not, the JS and the WASM no longer match: the browser fails at run time, or a new option has no effect. pnpm wasm:build:dev pnpm --filter wasm-html-to-image build # embed the WASM in the package again Native (host) tests​ The Mermaid engine (src/cpp/mermaid) is written with the standard library only, so the unit tests and the compatibility corpus run with the host compiler, without building the WASM. cmake --build build-host-tests --config Debug --target test_mermaid mermaid_cli ./build-host-tests/Debug/test_mermaid.exe # unit tests python tests/mermaid-corpus/run.py # 110 examples taken from the official documentation (exit status 1 on a new failure) mermaid_cli reads a diagram from standard input and writes the SVG. tests/mermaid-corpus/known-gaps.json lists the notations that are not supported yet. When you fix one, remove it from the list too (a fixed entry left in the list fails the run). About timings​ Times from the development build are longer than from the release build. When you record a timing (for example, how long a large flowchart takes to lay out), say which build you measured with.
